item.title: Bureau of Indian Affairs: Additional Actions Needed to Address Law Enforcement Staffing Challenges
item.description:
What GAO Found
The Department of the Interior and the Department of Justice (DOJ) fund law enforcement services on tribal lands through self-determination contracts, self-governance compacts, and competitive grants. Additionally, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) provides policing services directly to approximately 60 Tribes and provides specialized investigative services, such as units for drug enforcement and missing and murdered indigenous people, to all Tribes in conjunction with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). From 2016 through 2025, inflation-adjusted funding for contracts and compacts supporting law enforcement rose from $133,6 million to $137.5 million, while funding for law enforcement services BIA provides decreased from $40.8 million to $33.2 million.
As shown in the figure below, BIA has faced high vacancy rates for law enforcement officer positions on tribal lands. While BIA has taken some steps to address recruitment and retention challenges, BIA officials told GAO limited outreach to potential applicants, incentives, and housing options result in fewer applicants. Although the Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs has stated that strengthening tribal law enforcement is a top priority, BIA has not identified and implemented additional actions, such as expanding outreach and enhancing its incentive program. Without taking additional actions, BIA’s understaffing will likely persist, contributing to officer and community safety concerns.
Vacancy Rates for Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Law Enforcement Officers, September 2022–May 2025
Note: Vacancy rates, provided by BIA officials in January 2026, are a snapshot of vacant positions at the end of each fiscal year, with the exception of 2025, when rates were provided as of May.
Background investigations for BIA law enforcement officers are required to be conducted by the Department of Defense, absent statutory or delegated authority, which BIA officials said takes several months to a year. BIA officials said candidates may move on to other opportunities before the investigation is completed, further prolonging periods of understaffing. BIA officials said that the Bureau conducting its own background investigations would be more efficient, as it already does so within 30-45 days on average for law enforcement officers that Tribes hire. BIA has not pursued a delegation of this authority but could work with Interior’s Office of the Solicitor to request such authority from the Office of Personnel Management. Pursuing authority to conduct background investigations for BIA officers could enable BIA to more effectively fill vacant positions.
Why GAO Did This Study
According to DOJ, communities on tribal lands face persistent levels of violent crime and victimization. Law enforcement services on tribal lands have faced funding and staffing shortfalls for years, limiting their ability to respond to crime and improve public safety.
GAO was asked to review law enforcement personnel shortages on tribal lands. This report examines (1) how BIA and DOJ have provided funding and services for law enforcement on tribal lands, (2) the extent to which BIA has filled vacant positions for federal law enforcement officers on tribal lands, and (3) the challenges Tribes and BIA encounter with providing law enforcement services on tribal lands and the actions they have taken, if any, to address these challenges.
GAO analyzed funding and staffing data as well as policies and procedures, including BIA recruitment and retention guidance. GAO also interviewed officials, visited tribal lands in Maine and South Dakota, and conducted listening sessions with tribal advocacy organizations.
